spec_choices.why: The designer fixed 3-4 and suggested 4. Below 3 the n-1 Kododo threshold and the bust rule lose their tension, and there are only 4 bonus colours, so 4 is the maximum.

spec_choices.what: Keep the simultaneous talk poll before the plays
spec_choices.why: The rules require it. Players disagree about which colour should score, because each has a secret bonus colour, and coordinating exactly n-1 Kododos invites bluffing. A simultaneous poll with broadcast matches 'at the same time, without seeing the others'.
Each card needs a compact text form so hands can be lists and colour counts can be taken by first letter.
scored_cards can never exceed 14, so multiplying the score by 100 puts score first and scored cards second. Players still level share the win, which is the source's draw.

simplifications.what: Hands are visible only to their owner, while played cards are public
simplifications.why: This matches 'hands are private'. Tracking what others hold is left to the players, as the source intends.

simplifications.what: Reveal steps are tell steps over the public first_card and second_card
simplifications.why: Cards placed in a poll stay unseen until all answers are in, which is the face-down placement; the tell then reveals them.

variation.original_summary: 5211 is a 3-8 player simultaneous card game. Each round every player commits 4 cards from a hidden hand over three face-down turns. The most-played colour scores for the players who played it, unless it 'busts' by being played too much or is tied. A special Kododo count can override everything so that only Kododo players score.

review.evidence: No simple policy is safe. 'Always play your highest cards' piles onto whatever colour you hold most of, and that colour gets tied or busts. Two players following the same simple policy usually tie, which discards the colour. Play is simultaneous, so no seat has an edge.

Reading the table and timing bust risks is a real skill. But hands come from a 100-card shuffled deck with refills, and some cards are removed unseen. A player who draws a strong colour concentration or extra Kododos has a large edge that skill only partly offsets.

Deep play exists: steering the majority, predicting busts, holding Kododos for the exact-count round, using what was revealed in earlier turns. A weak player still scores whenever they happen to join the winning colour.
Hands are hidden and turns are simultaneous. Each player has to infer from earlier revealed cards what colours others are likely to play, and whether a colour is near busting.
Scoring is pure counting: the Kododo total, the per-colour counts, the bust threshold and the card values.

It is text-only and simultaneous. However, a 100-card shuffled deck, per-player refill draws every turn, three play turns and a cascading 'next most-played colour' rule exceed the one-random-draw-per-round and step limits. The game also runs long.

problems: Luck of the deal and of the per-turn refill draws strongly affects who can control a colour or hit the Kododo count. This is a lottery element.
Per-player refill draws every turn need several random draws per round, which the platform limits to one.
Three play turns per round plus five colour counts plus a cascading tie and bust resolution need too many steps.
The game length (a 100-card deck run down) is too long for the platform.
Hand contents are the only private information. Once hands are luck-driven, the hidden element measures luck more than intent.

changes.what: Every player gets an identical fixed 14-card hand: 4 colours each with values 1, 2 and 3, plus 2 Kododos. There is no deck and no refills.
changes.why: This removes hand luck entirely. Because played cards are public, a player who tracks the plays knows what everyone has left, so the contest is about predicting intent and timing.
changes.fixes: Luck of the deal and of the per-turn refill draws strongly affects who can control a colour or hit the Kododo count. This is a lottery element.

changes.what: Removed all in-game drawing. The only random event is a setup deal of distinct secret bonus colours.
changes.why: This fits the limit of at most one random draw per round.
changes.fixes: Per-player refill draws every turn need several random draws per round, which the platform limits to one.

changes.what: Each round is two simultaneous card plays: one face-down card, a reveal, then a second face-down card, then a reveal. This replaces the original three turns of 2+1+1 cards.
changes.why: It keeps the 'see part of the table, then commit more' tension in far fewer steps.
changes.fixes: Three play turns per round plus five colour counts plus a cascading tie and bust resolution need too many steps.

changes.what: Cut to 4 colours. Resolution is a single rule: the non-busted colour with the strictly highest count scores, and if the top is tied nothing scores.
changes.why: A single arithmetic comparison replaces the cascade. Ties still kill the colour, as in the original.
changes.fixes: Three play turns per round plus five colour counts plus a cascading tie and bust resolution need too many steps.

changes.what: The game is fixed at 7 rounds, so all 14 cards are played.
changes.why: This keeps it short. The forced endgame also rewards planning which cards to save.
changes.fixes: The game length (a 100-card deck run down) is too long for the platform.

changes.what: Each player gets a secret bonus colour, distinct from everyone else's, and earns +1 per scored card of that colour.
changes.why: It adds a symmetric hidden type. Each type has equal total value, but it changes which colours you want to win. Players must infer each other's bonus colours from their plays and talk.
changes.fixes: Hand contents are the only private information. Once hands are luck-driven, the hidden element measures luck more than intent.

changes.what: Added a simultaneous one-message talk phase before the first card each round.
changes.why: It allows bluffing and temporary alliances to swing a majority. Since only one player can win and players hold different bonus colours, proposals are self-interested and following one blindly can tie or bust a colour.
changes.fixes: Hand contents are the only private information. Once hands are luck-driven, the hidden element measures luck more than intent.

keeps: Simultaneous face-down card plays from a hidden hand
The most-played colour scores only for those who played it
The bust rule: a colour played too much scores nothing
Ties for the majority kill the tied colours
The Kododo override: an exact Kododo count lets only Kododo players score
Partial reveal mid-round, then further commitment
Highest total wins, with most scored cards as the tie-break

recommendation.reason: The core majority, bust and Kododo guessing game is strong and inference-heavy. Its problems are deal luck and size, and both can be fixed within the limits.

variation.name: 5211: Mirror Hands
variation.summary: Every player holds the same 14 cards and a secret bonus colour. Over 7 rounds they each commit two cards, one at a time, trying to be in the colour that wins the majority without busting it, or to hit the exact Kododo count.
variation.rules:
SETUP. Let n be the number of players (3 or 4). Every player receives an identical hand of 14 cards:
- the colours Red, Blue, Green and Yellow, each with values 1, 2 and 3 (12 cards);
- 2 Kododo cards, which have no colour and are worth 3 each.
Hands are private, but because every hand starts identical and all played cards are revealed, anyone can track what each player has left. Each player is then secretly dealt a bonus colour at random from Red, Blue, Green and Yellow, with no two players sharing one. Only that player knows it. Scores start at 0, and each player's scored-card count starts at 0.

EACH ROUND (7 rounds):
1. Talk. Every player writes one short message at the same time, without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone. Nothing said is binding.
2. First card. Every player at the same time places one card from their hand face down.
3. Reveal. All first cards are revealed.
4. Second card. Every player at the same time places one more card from their hand face down.
5. Reveal. All second cards are revealed. Played cards leave the hands.
6. Count. Count K, the number of Kododos played this round (out of 2n cards). Count how many cards of each colour were played.
7. Kododo check. If K equals exactly n-1 (2 Kododos with 3 players, 3 with 4 players), each player scores 3 points per Kododo they played this round and adds that many cards to their scored-card count. No colour scores this round.
8. Colour check (only if K is not exactly n-1). A colour is busted if its count is n+1 or more (4 or more with 3 players, 5 or more with 4 players). Among the colours that are not busted and have a count of at least 1, find the highest count. If exactly one colour has that highest count, it is the scoring colour. If two or more colours share it, or no colour qualifies, nothing scores this round.
   Each player scores the face values of their cards of the scoring colour, plus 1 extra point per such card if it is their bonus colour, and adds those cards to their scored-card count.
   Kododos played in a round where the Kododo check fails score nothing.
9. Announce the round result and the updated scores.

END. After round 7, all 14 cards have been played and the game ends.
variation.objective: The player with the highest total score wins. If players are tied on total score, the one among them with the higher scored-card count wins. If they are still tied, the game is a draw among the tied players.
variation.expected_effect:
Removing deal luck makes the result depend on predicting others' plays.

How the round plays: the mid-round reveal lets players react, either by joining the emerging leader or by deliberately pushing it to bust or tie. Kododo timing becomes a pure reading game, because everyone knows exactly how many Kododos each opponent has left.

What players disagree about: hidden bonus colours mean each player wants a different colour to win. Talk is used to propose a colour, recruit allies and bluff. A player who simply follows a proposal can lose in three ways: two others pile on and bust the colour, a rival splits the vote to force a tie, or the proposer benefits from the bonus while the follower gains only face value.

The endgame: the fixed 14-card hand rewards planning which high cards and Kododos to save for the late, fully deducible rounds.

balanced.evidence: There are no seats and no move order: every choice is a simultaneous poll, and all hands start identical. Each player holds 4 colours × (1+2+3) = 24 colour points plus 2 Kododos × 3 = 6, so 30 base points. A bonus colour adds at most +3 (one per card). Per-round payoffs for a two-card play: KK scores 6 if K hits n-1 exactly; a same-colour pair 3+2 scores 5, or 7 with the bonus; a single card scores 1-3 (+1 with the bonus). No option is strictly better whatever the others do. A KK play scores 0 if any opponent adds a Kododo, because then K=3 ≠ 2 with 3 players. A colour pair scores 0 if the colour busts (count ≥ n+1) or ties for highest. Thoughtless policies under the WINNER RULE: (a) 'Always the first listed card' (R1, R2, then R3, B1 …). Against itself, all 6 round-1 cards are red, count 6 ≥ 4, bust. Later rounds tie or bust in the same way, everyone scores 0, and the game is a draw. Against a sensible player it loses. The sensible player sees the thoughtless player's revealed first card and answers with whatever wins the colour majority, e.g. B3 then B2 alongside one other blue. Or it adds a red so that red scores only when its own red value is higher. Over 7 rounds the sensible player only plays into colours where its contribution is at least the thoughtless player's, and reaches about 25+ against about 15. (b) 'Dump both Kododos in round 1'. Against random play it scores 6 only if no opponent plays a Kododo. Each random opponent plays one with probability 1-(12/14·11/13) ≈ 0.27, so the dump fails about 1-0.73² ≈ 47% of the time with two opponents. Against sensible play it fails 100%. An opponent seeing the first revealed Kododo can answer with a K as its second card, making K=3, at a cost of 3 to itself against 6 to the dumper. (c) 'Always the highest value' plays the 3s early. That is readable from the open tracking, so opponents decide whether that colour busts, and it loses to sensible play. No thoughtless policy comes close to never losing, and every player can win. There is no labelled payoff ordering to contradict.

playable.evidence: The rules are complete. They specify the hands, the K = n-1 test, the bust threshold n+1, the unique-maximum rule among non-busted colours with count ≥ 1, the 'nothing scores' cases, the bonus +1 per card, the scored-card count, and the tie-break followed by a draw. The game is finite: exactly 14 cards over 7 rounds of 2. All scoring is arithmetic on counts and values the engine keeps. Complexity is within limits: steps 17 ≤ 20; choice steps 3 (talk, card 1, card 2) ≤ 4; attributes 14 ≤ 20; hidden elements 2 (hand, bonus) ≤ 3; random draws per round 0, since the bonus deal is a one-off at setup; rounds 7 ≤ 40. It needs no board, clock, trading or binding agreement. Hands use the supported hidden_hands feature. Talk is justified and simultaneous. Players disagree: each wants their own secret bonus colour to score, and players fight over whether a Kododo round succeeds. Following a proposal can cost you, for example by supporting a colour where the proposer has the 3 and you have the 1, or by adding the second Kododo that lets them score. Talk also gives material to reason about, such as bluffs about bonus colours. Late rounds are not a 'safe option wins' cooperation trap. The game is not a repeated dilemma, and the open tracking turns rounds 6-7 into computable endgames, which is planning rather than a dominant safe move.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: The only randomness is the setup deal of distinct bonus colours, worth at most +3 per player. It is symmetric: everyone gets one, and no colour is intrinsically better. With all players playing well, the result is decided by things players control. One is which colours each player steers into scoring with high cards rather than low ones. Another is how well each player infers opponents' bonus colours from talk and plays. A third is the mid-round response once first cards are revealed: block or join a Kododo round, bust a colour, or create a tie. A draw is not decided by chance. I estimate chance at under 15% of the outcome. There is real inference: the hidden bonus colour can be read from a player's preferences, and remaining hands can be tracked exactly. There is also a way to act on it: the second card is chosen after seeing the first cards, which allows bust and tie manipulation. A reasoning player clearly beats a careless one, as the policy tests above show.
